strengths: Well-executed and extensive empirical evaluation: 135 chaotic systems, 20 initial conditions per system, multiple metrics (sMAPE, VPT, MSE, MAE), multiple context lengths, and multiple state-of-the-art foundation models (Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM, Time-MoE), making the central claim—that a parameter-free parroting baseline beats foundation models at a fraction of the cost—convincingly supported.

The Nadaraya–Watson formulation of parroting is elegant and unifying, cleanly connecting the strategy to classical nonlinear forecasting (simplex projection, S-map), k-gram smoothing, and softmax attention, which situates the empirical findings in a solid theoretical framework.

The link between the in-context scaling exponent and the correlation dimension of the attractor (α = 1/d_cor), supported by a per-system correlation analysis across 135 systems, provides a genuinely interesting dynamical-systems explanation for previously observed in-context neural scaling laws.

The paper is honest about scope: it acknowledges where Chronos outperforms parroting (short contexts) and frames parroting as a baseline/diagnostic rather than overclaiming it as a method contribution.

Clear implications for the field: provides a tough-to-beat baseline that exposes limitations of current time-series foundation models and can inform benchmark design and the design of future models with strategies beyond parroting.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core mechanism is essentially classical analog/nearest-neighbor forecasting from nonlinear dynamics (Sugihara & May 1990; simplex projection), and the observation that Chronos parrots on chaotic systems was already established in prior work (Zhang & Gilpin [42]). The paper largely formalizes, extends, and re-frames this known result rather than introducing a fundamentally new idea.

The fractal-dimension scaling result, while nicely verified, is close to expected from standard ergodic theory: the L^{-1/d_cor} scaling of nearest-neighbor distances is a well-known consequence of sampling a fractal measure, so the theoretical contribution is more a synthesis than a new result. The empirical correlation (Spearman 0.44) is moderate and the fit visibly deviates from the 1:1 line.

The parroting algorithm is never directly benchmarked against its classical ancestors (simplex projection, S-map) in the main experiments, despite being shown to be a limiting case; it would strengthen the paper to show whether parroting's advantage over foundation models also holds for these decades-old baselines, which would further deflate the claimed surprise.

The claim that foundation models 'fail to develop meaningful representations of the underlying physics' is stronger than the evidence: the evaluation is limited to autonomous, stationary, low-dimensional chaotic ODE systems with dense sampling, a regime specifically favorable to motif-copying; no non-stationary, noisy, or real-world scientific time series are tested, and the authors themselves note Chronos wins at short contexts.

Practical relevance of the strongest result is questionable: parroting's advantage grows with context length (up to 32k points, ~1000 Lyapunov times), whereas the motivating use case for foundation models is short-context, data-limited forecasting where foundation models actually win.

Some technical presentation issues: notational inconsistencies between the main text (σ, D, L) and the appendix (h, L, C), an unresolved reference ('Eq. 5' cited before the appendix defining it), and typo-level errors (e.g., 'exact repetion', 'a Nadaraya–Watson'); the proposition in C.3 is essentially an informal derivation rather than a rigorous theorem with stated regularity conditions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: whether time-series foundation models (TSFMs) genuinely learn physics or exploit trivial copying strategies, and it makes this question concrete and testable.

The empirical benchmark is reasonably thorough: 135 chaotic systems from the dysts database, 20 initial conditions per system, multiple metrics (sMAPE, VPT, MSE, MAE), multiple context lengths, and four modern TSFMs (Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM, TimeMoE).

The finding that a parameter-free nearest-neighbor baseline outperforms all TSFMs at 5-6 orders of magnitude lower inference cost is a striking and useful calibration result for the community, and the paper frames it constructively as a baseline rather than merely a criticism.

The attempt to connect the in-context scaling law exponent to the attractor's correlation dimension is a genuinely interesting hypothesis that links neural scaling laws to invariant properties of the data-generating process.

The paper is well written and well organized, with helpful connections to induction heads, Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression, and classical nonlinear forecasting (simplex projection, S-map) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method: nearest-neighbor 'analog' forecasting of chaotic time series is decades old (Lorenz's analogue method; Sugihara & May 1990), and the paper's own Appendix C.2 concedes that context parroting is a special case/limit of simplex projection and S-map. The main new element is rebranding this classical technique as a 'baseline' and running it against TSFMs.

Heavy overlap with prior work: the key observation that Chronos forecasts chaotic systems by context parroting was already made by Zhang & Gilpin [42], the paper's own reference and apparent inspiration. This paper largely distills that observation into an explicit algorithm and scales up the evaluation; the conceptual contribution beyond [42] is incremental.

The headline theoretical claim linking the scaling exponent alpha to 1/d_cor is weakly supported: the reported Spearman correlation is only 0.44 +/- 0.08, which the text nonetheless characterizes as 'strong correlation.' The scatter in Fig. 7 deviates substantially from the 1:1 line, and the paper itself admits alpha is hard to estimate. The proposition in C.3 is essentially a consistency statement for kernel regression on ergodic systems and is fairly standard.

The comparison design somewhat favors the baseline: context parroting is allowed contexts up to 32768 points while several TSFMs are capped at 512-4096, and foundation models are evaluated zero-shot with no fine-tuning or adaptation to the chaotic-systems domain, even though the paper's own conclusion calls for domain fine-tuning. Fairness of the 'outperforms state-of-the-art' claim is limited by this asymmetry.

Despite extensively discussing simplex projection and S-map, the paper does not actually benchmark these classical methods in the main experiments, which would contextualize how much of the gain is simply 'old nonlinear forecasting beats TSFMs' versus anything new.

Scope is narrow: evaluation is confined to synthetic, stationary, deterministic low-dimensional ODE systems with univariate per-dimension forecasts. The generalization of the conclusions ('foundation models fail to extract physical insight') to SciML broadly, or to noisy/nonstationary real systems, is asserted but not demonstrated.

The mechanistic claims about why Chronos parrots (cross-entropy loss incentivizing k-gram preservation) are plausible but speculative and not directly verified via attention analysis or ablations on the models themselves.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated central finding: a training-free, parameter-free nearest-neighbor baseline (context parroting) outperforms three state-of-the-art time-series foundation models (Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM, Time-MoE) on zero-shot chaotic-system forecasting, at 5-6 orders of magnitude lower inference cost. This is a genuinely surprising and practically important result for the SciML community.

Broad and reasonably rigorous empirical evaluation: 135 chaotic systems from the dysts benchmark, 20 random initial conditions per system, multiple metrics (sMAPE, VPT, plus MSE/MAE in the appendix), systematic study of context length and embedding dimension, and honest reporting that Chronos beats parroting on short contexts.

Nice theoretical framing that connects the empirical phenomenon to established knowledge: Nadaraya-Watson / kernel-regression formulation, reduction to simplex projection and S-map in various limits, connection to induction heads, and a formal (if idealized) proposition that long-context parroting preserves invariants of ergodic systems.

The attempt to explain the in-context neural scaling law via the correlation dimension of the attractor (α = 1/d_cor) is a creative and potentially influential idea, linking observed scaling coefficients to an invariant physical property of the data-generating process.

Well-written paper with a clear narrative, useful figures (e.g., Fig. 8 qualitative forecasts showing MSE-trained models converging to the mean), and a forward-looking discussion connecting to the stochastic-parrots debate and better baseline design.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method: context parroting is essentially a 1-nearest-neighbor forecaster, closely related to simplex projection and analog methods from nonlinear dynamics dating to the 1990s (Sugihara & May), which the authors themselves acknowledge in Appendix C.2. Moreover, the observation that Chronos parrots is already established in prior work [42]; the main increment here is systematizing it as a baseline and adding the scaling-law analysis.

Missing empirical comparison to the most relevant baselines: while the paper shows theoretical reductions to simplex projection and S-map, it never benchmarks against these classical nonlinear forecasting methods (or even against classical deep learning models / domain-specific baselines from [42]). This weakens the 'tough-to-beat' claim—simplex projection with adaptive embedding might be competitive or better.

The central theoretical claim α = 1/d_cor is supported only by a moderate correlation (Spearman 0.44 ± 0.08) over 135 systems, with substantial scatter around the 1:1 line and acknowledged difficulty in estimating α. The derivation is heuristic (random-sampling assumption on the attractor, neglect of temporal correlation between motifs). The claim 'strong correlation' in the text overstates the evidence.

Scope is narrow: only chaotic, stationary, low-dimensional ODE systems; all forecasts are univariate per dimension. The conclusions about foundation models 'failing to develop meaningful representations' are drawn entirely from this regime and may not generalize to nonstationary real-world series where foundation models presumably excel; the authors concede this but the abstract/title claims are broader than the evidence.

Some technical presentation issues: inconsistent notation across the main text and appendix (L vs. C vs. D for context length and motif length; Eq. 1 in the main text restated as Eq. 5 in the appendix; 'exact repetion' typo; the C.3 proposition's kernel conditions are not made precise). The Nadaraya-Watson theory applies to the smoothed estimator, while the actual experiments use the σ→0 limit whose convergence properties are less controlled.

Reproducibility details are thin in the main text: no mention of released code, the distance normalization for multi-dimensional series, how context length interacts with the D-motif exclusion window, or hyperparameter choices for the foundation models (e.g., sampling settings for Chronos), which could affect the comparison.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed contribution: establishing context parroting as an explicit, tough-to-beat baseline for zero-shot forecasting of dynamical systems, which directly challenges the claimed capabilities of time-series foundation models in SciML.

Comprehensive and careful empirical evaluation: 135 chaotic systems (dysts), 20 random initial conditions per system, multiple complementary metrics (sMAPE, VPT, MAE, MSE, attractor KL divergence, correlation dimension), ablations over noise levels, sampling granularity, and embedding dimension, plus four real-world/high-dimensional tasks (von Kármán flow, ECG, electronic circuits, Kuramoto).

Valuable computational analysis showing 5–6 orders of magnitude inference-cost advantage, and the important finding that Chronos saturates at its designed context length while parroting keeps improving with context length.

Nice theoretical tie-in connecting the in-context neural scaling exponent to the correlation dimension of the chaotic attractor (α = 1/d_cor), and reproducing the in-context scaling law of Liu et al. via a simple, interpretable mechanism.

Useful mechanistic framing: connecting parroting to induction heads offers a plausible explanation for why text-trained LLMs transfer to time series, and the identification of a shared failure mode (converging to the mean) across TimesFM, TimeMoE, and Chronos Bolt is actionable for model design.

Honest scoping: the authors are explicit that the goal is a baseline/diagnostic rather than a replacement for foundation models, and they propose concrete benchmark-design ideas (un-parrotable initial conditions).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core method is essentially a 1-nearest-neighbor motif copy in delay-embedded space, equivalent in known limits to simplex projection, S-map, and Farmer–Sidorowich (1987) from nonlinear dynamics, and the observation that Chronos parrots chaotic systems was already made in prior work [42]. The paper primarily repackages and benchmarks these known ideas rather than introducing fundamentally new methodology.

Missing the most informative comparison: classical baselines (simplex projection, S-map, Farmer–Sidorowich) are discussed but not actually benchmarked against foundation models in the main experiments, even though these comparisons are the natural test of whether parroting is genuinely competitive or simply rediscovered classical forecasting.

The theoretical results are informal: the 'proposition' on preserving ergodic invariants is a heuristic kernel-regression limit argument rather than a rigorous theorem, and the link between α and 1/d_cor is supported only by a moderate Spearman correlation (0.51) across systems, leaving the central scaling-law claim only partially validated.

Some claims exceed the evidence: the induction-head parallel is speculative (no mechanistic analysis of foundation models' attention is performed), and the suggestion to estimate a 'fractal dimension' of language is mentioned without support.

Scope of evaluation is univariate per-dimension forecasting with normalized trajectories; behavior on nonstationary series, multivariate coupled forecasting, and longer prediction horizons in real tasks remains limited, which the authors acknowledge but which constrains the generality of the 'tough-to-beat' claim.
Significance is somewhat niche: the impact is mainly on the SciML/chaotic-forecasting community and benchmark design, rather than a broad methodological advance for the wider AI audience.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the comparison spans 135 chaotic systems from the dysts benchmark plus real-world datasets (ECG, electronic circuits, Kuramoto oscillators, von Kármán flow), with a diverse set of metrics (sMAPE, VPT, MSE, MAE, attractor KL divergence, correlation dimension) and ablations over noise, sampling granularity, context length, and embedding dimension.

The computational cost analysis (Fig. 3) is valuable and rarely reported: a five-to-six order of magnitude inference gap between parroting and foundation models is a striking and practically relevant finding.

The paper is well written and clearly motivated. Framing parroting as an explicit baseline to diagnose whether foundation models actually use context (vs. regressing to the mean, Fig. 6) is a useful contribution to benchmark design in SciML.

The unification in Appendix F (Nadaraya–Watson formulation connecting parroting to simplex projection, S-map, k-NN, and attention) provides a nice conceptual bridge between classical nonlinear dynamics and modern time-series foundation models.
The observation that Chronos saturates at its pre-training context length while parroting scales with arbitrary context (Fig. 4) is an interesting and actionable insight.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty. Context parroting is a nearest-neighbor lookup over delay-embedded motifs, essentially a continuous version of analog forecasting, simplex projection, and Farmer–Sidorowich (1987). The paper itself concedes equivalence in limits (Appendix F.2), so the central 'method' is a repackaging of decades-old ideas; the contribution is mainly empirical diagnosis rather than a new technique.

Missing key baselines. Despite explicitly deriving the connection to simplex projection and S-map, the paper never benchmarks against these classical nonlinear forecasting methods, nor against simple statistical baselines (Seasonal Naive, trend extrapolation), nor against other zero-shot models (TimeGPT, Lag-Llama, Moirai). Without these, it is unclear whether parroting's advantage is over modern deep models specifically or simply that the tasks reward any motif-copying scheme.

The evaluation design partially favors the proposed baseline. The primary benchmark (dysts) consists of low-dimensional chaotic systems with strong recurrences in state space—precisely the regime where copying motifs is near-optimal. The claim that foundation models 'underutilize context' is only supported on this narrow task family; the high-dimensional real-world results (Tables 1–3) are noticeably weaker, with parroting losing to TimesFM on electronic-circuit KL divergence and to TimeMoE on von Kármán, undermining the generality of the headline claim.

The theoretical scaling-law result is derivative and weakly supported. The link α = 1/d_cor was already derived for Farmer–Sidorowich forecasting (the authors cite this), and the empirical validation is modest: Spearman correlation of only 0.51 ± 0.08 between 1/α and d_cor (Fig. 11) with substantial scatter. The consistency proposition in F.3 is essentially a standard ergodic/consistency argument for Nadaraya–Watson estimators rather than a new result.

The connection to induction heads (Section 2, Section 5.2) is speculative. The paper proposes that parroting 'explains' why LLMs can be repurposed for time series, but provides no mechanistic evidence from any actual model (no attention analysis, no probing); this claim is stated in the abstract without direct support.

The choice of only four foundation models, with fixed context length 512 in the main comparison, limits the strength of the conclusions; at short contexts the paper itself shows Chronos outperforms parroting, which complicates the 'tough-to-beat' framing of the title.

Only three baselines considered beyond Chronos variants (the title claim rests heavily on Chronos's known parroting behavior from prior work [42]), leaving the incremental novelty over that prior observation unclear.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated central message: a trivially simple, computationally cheap baseline (context parroting) outperforms leading time-series foundation models on chaotic system forecasting, exposing real gaps in current models and providing actionable guidance for benchmark and model design.

Comprehensive and carefully designed evaluation: 135 chaotic systems from the dysts benchmark, 20+ random initial conditions, multiple complementary metrics (sMAPE, VPT, MAE, MSE, attractor KL divergence, correlation dimension), ablations over context length, embedding dimension, noise levels, and data granularity, plus four additional real-world/simulation SciML tasks (von Kármán, ECG, circuits, Kuramoto).

Useful theoretical framing: the Nadaraya–Watson formulation unifies parroting with classical nonlinear forecasting methods (simplex projection, S-map), a formal proposition showing parroting preserves ergodic invariants at long context, and a geometric explanation (α = 1/d_cor) of the in-context neural scaling law connecting forecast accuracy to attractor fractal dimension.

Meaningful connection to interpretability literature: the analogy between parroting and induction heads offers a plausible mechanistic account of why text-trained LLMs transfer to time-series forecasting without fine-tuning.

Thorough and honest analysis of failure modes (regression-to-the-mean for MSE-trained models, context saturation in Chronos) and candid acknowledgment of the baseline's own limitations (worse on short contexts, ties to Farmer–Sidorowich scaling result).
Good writing, clear figures, and reproducible methodology; the near-zero inference cost of parroting relative to foundation models is well documented (Fig. 3).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core observation that Chronos parrots was already made in prior work [42], and the scaling coefficient α = 1/d_cor is acknowledged to be a known derivation for the Farmer–Sidorowich method [77]. The paper is largely a distillation and systematization of these observations rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The proposed baseline is essentially a 1-nearest-neighbor variant of classical simplex projection in delay-embedding space, a technique from 1990 [74]; yet simplex projection and S-map are never empirically compared against parroting or the foundation models, despite the claimed theoretical equivalence. This missing classical baseline weakens the claim that parroting is 'tough-to-beat.'

The empirical support for the central theoretical claim (α = 1/d_cor) is relatively weak: Spearman correlation of only ~0.51 with substantial scatter in Fig. 11, and the authors concede numerical estimation is difficult. A more convincing quantitative validation would be expected.

The induction-head parallel is speculative; no experiments (e.g., attention analysis, ablations on LLM-based forecasters) directly substantiate that LLM forecasting behavior is explained by induction-head-like copying.

Only four foundation models are compared, all decoder/encoder-decoder point forecasters; newer or stronger models and additional strategies (e.g., fine-tuned models, classical deep forecasters like reservoir computing) are absent, limiting the breadth of the 'beats foundation models' claim.

Some claims are broader than the evidence: statements about guiding the design of future foundation models and replacing Naive/Seasonal Naive baselines for general time series remain largely aspirational; generalization beyond stationary/chaotic regimes is not demonstrated.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written paper that introduces context parroting as a transparent, nearly free baseline for zero-shot forecasting of dynamical systems, following the useful tradition of 'simple but tough-to-beat baselines' (e.g., Arora et al. 2017).

Extensive and well-designed empirical evaluation: 135 chaotic systems from the dysts benchmark, multiple state-of-the-art foundation models (Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM-2.0, Time-MoE, Moirai-2.0, DynaMix), diverse metrics (sMAPE, MSE, MAE, attractor KL divergence, power spectrum Hellinger distance, correlation dimension, Lyapunov exponents), and thorough ablations (noise levels, sampling granularity, embedding dimension, context length, long-horizon rollouts).
Goes beyond toy ODEs to real-world scientific datasets (turbulence, ECG, experimental coupled circuits, Kuramoto networks), showing the findings generalize across SciML tasks.

Interesting theoretical contribution linking the in-context neural scaling exponent to the fractal (correlation) dimension of the attractor (α = 1/d_cor), providing a mechanistic explanation for previously observed scaling laws for LLMs on dynamical systems, with empirical support (Spearman ~0.85).

Honest and careful framing: the authors explicitly note that parroting 'games' reconstruction metrics, that Chronos uses additional strategies on short contexts, and that the goal is to expose gaps in foundation models rather than to replace them; the connection to induction heads is clearly presented as a hypothesis.
Reproducibility statement with code release; the method itself is trivially implementable, supporting its use as a community baseline.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: context parroting is essentially a 1-nearest-neighbor lookup in delay-embedding space, closely related to (and shown by the authors to reduce to) simplex projection and Farmer–Sidorowich methods from 1987–1990; the observation that Chronos parrots was already reported by Zhang & Gilpin (2024). The main new elements are the systematic benchmarking and the scaling-law analysis.

The headline theoretical result α = 1/d_cor is largely a restatement of known nearest-neighbor sampling results for Farmer–Sidorowich forecasting (which the authors acknowledge), so the theoretical contribution is modest; the derivation assumes ergodicity and clean deterministic ODEs, and applicability to stochastic systems (where the original scaling law was observed) remains open.

The benchmark design inherently favors parroting: context and forecast come from the same long, deterministic, stationary trajectory sampled at 30 points per Lyapunov time, so near-verbatim motifs almost surely exist. This weakens the generality of the claim that foundation models 'fail to learn the underlying physics'; performance on genuinely nonstationary or noisy real-world forecasting (the intended use case of these models) is only briefly touched.

Some comparisons may be slightly unfair: foundation models are evaluated via median predictions (discarding distributional information that is central to chaos forecasting), fixed context-length limits (e.g., Chronos at 512) constrain some models while parroting scales freely, and the univariate per-dimension evaluation ignores multivariate structure that some models exploit.
Statistical support for the scaling-law claim is correlational only (scatter plot, Spearman 0.85); no controlled experiment varying attractor dimension independently to verify α = 1/d_cor.

The induction-head parallel and the suggestion that parroting explains LLM scaling laws are speculative and largely qualitative; the observed Lyapunov-exponent correlation for parroting is weak (0.343), indicating imperfect preservation of dynamics in practice.

The references section is very long relative to the technical content, and some citations (e.g., Chronos-2, Moirai 2.0, Sundial) suggest rapidly moving target models, which may date the empirical conclusions quickly.

strengths: Extensive empirical benchmarking across 135 chaotic systems (dysts), plus ECG, circuit, turbulence, and Kuramoto datasets, with a broad set of metrics (sMAPE, MSE, MAE, attractor KL divergence, power spectra, fractal dimension, Lyapunov exponents) and many strong baselines including Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM-2.0, Time-MoE, Moirai-2.0, and DynaMix
The observation that leading time-series foundation models regress to the mean and fail to fully exploit context is a useful caution for the SciML community

The paper includes noise, sampling-rate granularity, and embedding-dimension ablations, and derives formal properties of parroting (Nadaraya–Watson limits, connection to simplex projection and S-map) in the appendix
weaknesses: Limited novelty: 'context parroting' is essentially a 1-nearest-neighbor search in a time-delay embedding space, a technique known since the 1980s-90s (Farmer & Sidorowich 1987; Sugihara & May 1990). The paper itself acknowledges simplex projection and S-map as near-equivalents. The observation that Chronos parrots chaotic systems was already made by Zhang & Gilpin (2024), which this work builds directly on; the incremental contribution is mainly distilling the strategy into a baseline and running a benchmark

The central theoretical result, the scaling exponent α = 1/d_cor, is explicitly noted by the authors to follow from known results for the Farmer-Sidorowich method (Farmer & Sidorowich, 1987). Thus the 'theoretical explanation of in-context neural scaling laws' largely restates classical nonlinear dynamics results in new vocabulary, with Spearman correlation 0.85 as only empirical support and no rigorous derivation of the mapping from motif distance to one-step forecast error

The claimed connection to induction heads in LLMs is speculative and unvalidated; no experiments on actual attention patterns or mechanistic evidence are provided to support the assertion that parroting explains LLM zero-shot time-series ability

Unfair comparison framing: foundation models are evaluated zero-shot at their designed context limits (e.g., Chronos capped at 512) while parroting is allowed arbitrary context lengths; the six-orders-of-magnitude compute claim is unsurprising for comparing a pretrained 200M-parameter model to an O(DL) lookup, and ignores the training cost asymmetry discussion

The finding is largely confined to deterministic, stationary, self-repeating systems where copying from context is expected to succeed; results on nonstationary or real-world noisy tasks (e.g., ECG, turbulence) show mixed rankings (TimeMoE/Moirai beat parroting on turbulence MAE), somewhat weakening the 'tough-to-beat baseline' narrative

Writing and positioning oversell a repackaged classical method: claims such as a baseline that 'cannot be beat' or that non-beating models 'failed to learn the underlying physics' are stronger than the evidence, and the paper would benefit from a more measured contribution statement
Practical impact is unclear: the paper proposes no improved model, no modified benchmark beyond pointing out parroting can game metrics, and defers all constructive directions to future work

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: the paper benchmarks context parroting against five state-of-the-art time-series foundation models (Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM-2.0, Time-MoE, Moirai-2.0) plus DynaMix, AutoARIMA, and simplex projection, across 135 chaotic systems from the dysts benchmark with 20 random initial conditions per system, and across multiple complementary metrics (sMAPE, MSE, MAE, attractor KL divergence, power spectrum Hellinger distance, fractal dimension, Lyapunov exponents, valid prediction time).

The theoretical contribution connecting the in-context neural scaling exponent to the fractal (correlation) dimension of the attractor (α = 1/d_cor, validated by Spearman correlation ≈0.85) is genuinely insightful and provides a mechanistic explanation for an empirical phenomenon reported in prior work (Liu et al., 2024a).
The parallel drawn between context parroting and induction heads is well-motivated and provides a plausible mechanistic account of why LLM-based forecasters succeed on chaotic systems.

Careful experimental design: normalizing difficulty via Lyapunov times, aggregating over systems/dimensions/initial conditions, ablations on embedding dimension D, noise robustness, and sampling-rate granularity all strengthen the empirical claims.

Clear positioning and honest framing: the paper does not claim parroting should replace foundation models but rather serves as an informative diagnostic baseline, and it identifies concrete failure modes (regression to the mean in MSE-trained models) of current foundation models.

The Nadaraya–Watson formulation in the appendix elegantly unifies parroting with classical methods (simplex projection, S-map) and attention mechanisms, and the ergodicity-based proposition that parroting preserves invariant measures is a nice theoretical grounding.
Good reproducibility potential: the algorithm is fully specified (Algorithm 1), standard public benchmarks and pretrained models are used, and a code release is promised.
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: the central observation—that Chronos forecasts chaotic systems by copying from context—was already made by Zhang & Gilpin (2024), and the paper itself acknowledges that context parroting is essentially equivalent to classical nonlinear forecasting methods (simplex projection, S-map, Farmer-Sidorowich) from the 1980s–1990s. The main contribution is thus a rigorous benchmarking and analysis of a known technique rather than a new method.

The scaling-law result α = 1/d_cor closely mirrors the well-known nearest-neighbor sample-density argument from Farmer & Sidorowich (1987), which the paper cites; the theoretical novelty over that 35-year-old derivation is incremental, mainly reinterpreting it as an explanation of LLM in-context scaling.

Scope of the empirical claims: the headline result (parroting beats foundation models) is demonstrated primarily on deterministic low-dimensional chaotic ODEs where stationarity and recurrence make copying effective; the real-world extensions (ECG, circuits, Kuramoto, turbulence) in Tables 1–3 show mixed results (e.g., Parrot is not best on Turbulence MAE/MSE or on several KL-divergence entries), which somewhat weakens the generality of the 'tough-to-beat baseline' claim.

Some comparisons may be somewhat unfair or incomplete: several foundation models were not designed for chaotic dynamics, and the paper does not test stronger recent models (e.g., Chronos-2, which is cited but apparently not benchmarked) or fine-tuned variants that might close the gap.

The mechanism linking Chronos's parroting behavior to induction heads remains speculative—no direct mechanistic analysis (e.g., attention-head inspection) of any foundation model is performed to substantiate the claimed parallel.

The theoretical proposition on invariant preservation holds only in the double limit of infinite context and vanishing kernel bandwidth for ergodic systems; the gap between this idealized setting and practical finite-context behavior (where parroting outputs periodic trajectories) is acknowledged but not fully quantified.
The reproducibility statement contains an empty URL; the code link must be provided for the reproducibility claims to be verifiable.

Discussion of failure cases where parroting fails (e.g., strongly non-stationary or weakly stochastic systems) is deferred to future work, leaving the boundary conditions of the method's effectiveness underexplored.
